visualVerification.source: H:/Ancient Japan History/ch1/ch1.pdf and the thirty paired-page WebP exports
visualVerification.method: Full contact-sheet review plus direct inspection of the opening, Middle Jomon, Yayoi burial, and final summary spreads; OCR checked for headings, chronology, maps, quotations, and material claims.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 48-50; OCR opening through the pre-Jomon heading
substanceRetained: The distinction between retrospective court chronicles, Chinese external testimony, and archaeology.
The caution against treating Jomon, Yayoi, or later Yamato as a ready-made national identity.
omittedAs: Bibliographic apparatus
The source's dated racial ranking language
supplementalSources: ch01-research-notes.md: modern treatment of evidence categories and population history.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 50-53; OCR Late Paleolithic geography, fauna, loam, Iwajuku, and Kanto occupation
substanceRetained: Changing straits, continental connections, volcanic deposits, repeated Kanto occupation, stone procurement, and ecological change.
The source's insistence that early occupation claims require securely associated artifacts and dates.
omittedAs: Long species catalogues
Full bibliography and obsolete site claims
supplementalSources: ch01-research-notes.md: secure occupation after reassessment of the Early Paleolithic record.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 53-58; OCR final Paleolithic, Mesolithic, cave sequences, bow and arrow, pottery, and microblades
substanceRetained: Environmental warming, changes in prey, composite and projectile technologies, early pottery, cave sequences, and northern Asian microblade connections.
The relationship between containers, food processing, and repeated use of places.
omittedAs: Individual uncalibrated measurements and footnotes

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 58-63; OCR Earliest Jomon, Natsushima, Hanawadai, regional pottery, site distribution, and Map 1.1
substanceRetained: Jomon as a regional chronological convention, coastal adaptation, shell middens, small communities, and regional ceramic variation.
The environmental and chronological diversity obscured by a single national sequence.
omittedAs: Exact outdated population totals
Map labels reproduced in the web atlas instead

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 63-66; OCR Early Jomon warming, Minabori, Torihama, storage, wood, basketry, lacquer, and plants
substanceRetained: Sea-level change, Early Jomon villages, storage, house construction, Torihama's perishable materials, and the question of plant management.
omittedAs: Specialist botanical nomenclature where it does not change the argument

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 66-70; OCR Middle Jomon mountains, nuts and roots, pit dwellings, population concentration, pottery, and exchange
substanceRetained: Central-mountain settlement, nut and root processing, storage, house rebuilding, hearths, regional pottery, and obsidian exchange.
The source's competing explanations for Middle Jomon concentration, presented as hypotheses rather than facts.
omittedAs: Detailed cultivar/species lists
Site-by-site catalogue material

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 70-75; OCR figurines, stone objects, ritual houses, Late Jomon coast, fishing, canoes, and seasonal subsistence
substanceRetained: Managed food systems, seasonal coastal work, watercraft, figurines, ritual deposits, and the limits of interpretation.
omittedAs: The source's unsupported fixed readings of fertility and gender symbols

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 75-81; OCR Late and Final Jomon pottery, cemeteries, stone circles, regional contraction, and continental contacts
substanceRetained: Mortuary practice, ritual landscapes, changing settlement patterns, regional contraction, and selective continental connections.
omittedAs: Exhaustive artifact typologies
Claims that make climate a single universal cause

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 81-86; OCR early Yayoi cultivation, paddies, settlements, defense, burial, and Map 1.2
substanceRetained: Rice cultivation, water control, settlement organization, storage, violence, burial differentiation, and the regional nature of the Yayoi transition.
omittedAs: The former conventional date for the beginning of rice cultivation
Map labels reproduced in the web atlas instead
supplementalSources: ch01-research-notes.md: tenth-century BC chronology for northern Kyushu rice cultivation.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 86-94; OCR Yayoi burials, bronze weapons, bells, workshops, mirrors, and regional ritual distributions
substanceRetained: Burial differentiation, metal production and circulation, dotaku, weapon-shaped bronzes, mirrors, ritual deposition, and regional political fields.
omittedAs: Long mold and alloy technical lists
Claims that stylistic zones were fixed ethnic territories

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 94-99; OCR Chinese accounts, Himiko, Yamatai itinerary, customs, and trade
substanceRetained: Chinese court framing, Wa polities, Yamatai, Himiko, the disputed route, divination, weaving, and the convergence of diplomacy and local hierarchy.
omittedAs: The source's certainty about the location of Yamatai
Sensational casualty and attendant numbers treated as uncorroborated court reporting
supplementalSources: ch01-research-notes.md: Chinese testimony kept distinct from contemporary archaeological evidence.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 99-103; OCR trade, tools, salt, language hypotheses, skeletal discussion, population, and late Yayoi leadership
substanceRetained: The breadth of Yayoi exchange, regional craft and transport, the limits of linguistic inference, social differentiation, and the political importance of regional centers.
omittedAs: Racial typologies and typological physical rankings
Unsupported language-origin conclusions
supplementalSources: ch01-research-notes.md: ancient genomic evidence and regional admixture framework.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF pp. 103-107; OCR Izumo, Kojindani, Tsukushi, court myth, Sujin, and the source conclusion
substanceRetained: Izumo's material power, Kōjindani, regional political competition, the distinction between court myth and archaeology, and the threshold to Kofun and Yamato.
omittedAs: Later shrine architectural history
The source's retrospective certainty about individual rulers
